extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, curriculum developers, and advanced graduate students interested in proof and proving
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly review of research on the teaching and learning of mathematical proof, summarizing definitional standards, theoretical constructs, empirical findings, and implications for classroom instruction and research. The chapter organizes work into perspectives (problem-solving, convincing, socially-embedded) and discusses pedagogical and assessment implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proof (classroom-community view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof is a mathematical argument, a connected sequence of assertions for or against a mathematical claim, that (1) uses statements accepted by the classroom community that are true and available without further justification; (2) employs forms of reasoning that are valid and known to, or within the conceptual reach of, the classroom community; and (3) is communicated with forms of expression that are appropriate and known to, or within the conceptual reach of, the classroom community. (Stylianides, 2007b)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite definition to judge whether an argument meets the classroom standard of proof: check the accepted premises, the validity/appropriateness of reasoning modes, and the representational/communicative forms. The terms 'true,' 'valid,' and 'appropriate' are to be interpreted in the context of contemporary mathematics and the specific classroom community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the multiple functions of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof can serve verification/falsification, explanation (insight into why an assertion is true), discovery (inventing new results), illustrating new methods of deduction, justifying the use of a definition or an axiom system, and communication (conveying results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing tasks or evaluating proofs, consider which function(s) the proof is intended to serve; different instructional aims (e.g., conveying insight vs. formal verification) may call for different forms of proof or supportive activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate proof across the curriculum (expectations in standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curriculum frameworks (e.g., Common Core; National Mathematics Curriculum in England) call for an important role of proof at all ages: students should 'reason mathematically by following a line of enquiry, conjecturing relationships and generalisations, and developing an argument, justification or proof using mathematical language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction and assessments that provide opportunities for conjecturing, generalizing, and developing arguments/proofs from early grades onward; situate proof within broader mathematical activities rather than isolating it as a separate topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof production: normative correctness and producibility
rubrics_metrics.description: From the problem-solving perspective, desirable student outcomes include the ability to provide correct, normatively acceptable proofs or to determine correctness of purported proofs; the emphasis is often on processes of producing proofs (proof production/construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both the product (is the written argument a proof by disciplinary standards?) and process (what strategies were used?) — instructional interventions can target procedural/formal aspects as well as creative problem-centered aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal-rhetorical and problem-centered aspects of proving
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal-rhetorical part focuses on logical structuring and choice/implementation of a proof framework; the problem-centered part concerns creative decision-making and generating key insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and assessment should address both aspects: teach procedures for implementing proof frameworks (unpacking definitions, handling logical forms) and provide practice in heuristic/strategic insight generation (choosing proof methods, identifying key ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and implement an appropriate proof framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Provers must select legitimate methods (e.g., direct proof, proof by contradiction, proof by cases) and unpack the logical structure of statements (including handling nested conditionals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should check whether the chosen framework is logically appropriate for the statement; instruction should include guidance on when and how to select frameworks and on unpacking logical form (e.g., nested conditionals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and correctly use quantifiers and existence statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often mishandle quantifiers and existential statements (e.g., incorrectly reusing symbols for different existential objects; failing to recognize dependency of existential variables on universal variables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs for correct quantifier scope and variable dependency. Teach explicit strategies and representational habits for handling multiple quantifiers (e.g., careful notation, verbalization of dependencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridge informal and formal reasoning (semantic vs. syntactic productions; cognitive unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful proving often requires moving from informal, diagrammatic, or example-based reasoning (semantic/proofs based on key ideas) to formal syntactic proofs; cognitive unity denotes continuity between conjecturing processes and the proof used to verify the conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging student work, examine whether informal insights have been legitimately translated into formal warrants; instruction should cultivate syntactifying, elaborating, and rewarranting practices to reduce the structural distance between informal argument and formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective use of diagrams and examples (with awareness of pitfalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams and examples can facilitate understanding, generate ideas, and help complete subtasks, but they can also give false confidence, hide unstated assumptions, or leave students unclear about what must be proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should note whether diagrams/examples are used to generate legitimate insight and whether students make explicit the warrants that justify generalization; instruction should teach how to extract valid warrants from diagrams/examples and how to avoid overgeneralizing from insufficient cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate informal arguments into proofs (syntactifying, elaborating, rewarranting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key productive activities for translating informal arguments into formal proofs include syntactifying (expressing informal claims in precise language), elaborating (making explicit the principles used), and rewarranting (providing logical backing for graphical inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these process labels as assessment rubrics for students' ability to formalize reasoning; interventions can scaffold each activity explicitly when moving from examples/diagrams to proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof validation (reading and checking proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Validating a proof requires recognizing invalid proof frameworks (e.g., proofs that assume the conclusion), inferring the warrants or principles used to derive claims, and attending to the global structure of the argument rather than only local calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include validation tasks in assessment (present purported proofs and ask students to evaluate them); teach students to look for warrants and to test whether the framework logically yields the conclusion (spotting converse-errors, hidden assumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proof from invalid arguments (common invalid patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students (and some teachers) frequently accept invalid arguments such as proving the converse instead of the implication, or assuming the conclusion; inability to detect these stems from focusing on local computations rather than global argument structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment criteria should explicitly flag these invalid patterns; instruction should demonstrate counterexamples and require students to justify why a pattern is invalid (and how to repair it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Align students' standards of conviction with disciplinary standards (proving as convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the convincing perspective, instruction aims for students to be convinced by deductive arguments (not empirical evidence or appeals to authority), i.e., to adopt conviction standards closer to mathematicians'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and discussions that contrast empirical/authority-based justifications with deductive proofs; assess students' justificatory standards (surveys/interviews or classroom discourse) and support development toward deductive justification schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and classify argument types (Balacheff hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balacheff's hierarchy distinguishes argument types regarded as important in cognitive development: (1) naïve empiricism (few confirming cases), (2) crucial experiment (carefully selected cases), (3) generic example (operations on a representative case), and (4) thought experiment (internalized action detached from a particular representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to analyze what forms of argument students offer and to design tasks that move students from empirical or example-based reasoning toward more general, transformational reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify students' justification schemes (Harel & Sowder classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harel & Sowder classify justification schemes into: (1) externally-based (authority, ritual, non-referential symbol manipulation), (2) empirical (example- or perception-based), and (3) deductive/analytic (transformational or axiomatic justification schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating students' arguments, categorize their justificatory schemes to diagnose epistemic stances and to guide instruction aimed at shifting justificatory practices toward deductive/analytic schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand proof as socially-embedded and norm-governed
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument becomes a proof after social acceptance by a community; classroom sociomathematical norms (what counts as acceptable justification) shape students' proof production and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess classroom practices and norms as part of any evaluation of students' proofs; interventions should attend to establishing norms that privilege appropriate warrants and shared standards for acceptable proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design classroom opportunities and tasks that support proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunities include tasks that encourage conjecturing, generalizing, use of examples/diagrams, and discussion; teachers need to orchestrate productive mathematical discussions and create norms for justification and argumentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use task design and facilitation practices (e.g., 'five practices' for orchestrating discussion) as criteria for judging instruction quality; evaluate whether lessons create space for students to generate warrants, critique arguments, and refine proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher knowledge for facilitating proof activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers require content knowledge about proofs and pedagogical knowledge for engaging students in proving (e.g., understanding types of student difficulties, how to scaffold syntactifying/elaborating/rewarranting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess teacher readiness by examining their ability to interpret student arguments, design tasks that target specific proof competencies, and guide classroom discussions toward appropriate warrants and norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention-oriented instruction: research and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a pressing need for intervention-oriented, classroom-based studies that build on existing theoretical and empirical foundations to elevate the role of proof in ordinary classrooms and to support teachers' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating interventions, ensure they are theory-informed, target identified competencies (e.g., validation, quantifiers, syntactifying), and include measures of both student performance and changes in classroom norms/practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment and measurement of proving competence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is currently no widely used shared instrument for measuring students' proof-writing competence; existing studies use diverse tasks, making cross-study comparisons difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and use shared, validated measures that separate constructs (e.g., production vs. validation, formal vs. informal bridging) to allow reliable assessment of instructional interventions and population differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tasks that cluster proving with related activities (generalizing, conjecturing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving should be situated within a cluster of activities — generalizing, conjecturing, exploring examples — which often serve as precursors to proof and can provide meaningful contexts for developing proof competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tasks for whether they naturally elicit conjecture and generalization and whether they scaffold transitions from case-based reasoning to general proof; encourage tasks that make warrants explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for domain- and tool-specific argument types (e.g., dynamic geometry visual-variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some frameworks and argument types are specific to domains or tools (e.g., visual-variations in dynamic geometry environments) and may require specialized analytic categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing student arguments in specialized contexts, use or adapt frameworks suited to the domain or tool (e.g., include visual-variation categories for dynamic geometry tasks) rather than applying general rubrics uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and comprehending proofs: inferential and epistemic demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehension of proofs involves inferring implicit warrants, understanding the role of sources, and forming conviction; models of proof comprehension are being developed to assess reading ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include proof-reading and comprehension tasks (e.g., identifying warrants, explaining why steps follow) in assessment; use comprehension frameworks to diagnose where students fail (e.g., missing warrants, misreading sources).
